guidance.evidence_criterion: Read the complete definition, every alternative route into protection, form rules, and the operative nondisclosure duty. For explicit identification, support requires an identification, marking, description, or confirmation regime covering every protected route; contextual identification can qualify, but a separate blanket, nature-based, circumstances-based, or reasonable-person catchall that protects unidentified information opposes the all-information claim. A list of examples is not itself an identification requirement. For technical-only scope, oppose only when the definition expressly includes identifiable non-technical subjects such as business, financial, personnel, contractual, customer, or marketing information; generic references to confidential, proprietary, non-public, or business-related information alone leave exclusivity unresolved. Oral coverage requires express oral, verbal, visual, observed, or comparable non-tangible disclosure language, or an oral-confirmation rule; do not infer it from a substantive information category or general communications. Agreement-confidentiality requires the agreement, its contents, contractual arrangements or communications, negotiations, or their existence to fall under an operative nondisclosure duty; contemplated discussions alone are insufficient. An express permission covering the same subject opposes the relevant prohibition; otherwise return NotMentioned. Cite the governing opening, responsive alternatives, terminal modality, and operative duty only when each changes the result; exclude illustrative categories unrelated to the tested boundary.

Separate trigger, actor, disposition command, retention route, and survival. Return-or-destroy support requires termination, expiration, failure to proceed, cessation of services or the stated business purpose, or another express end-of-relationship event to activate a duty; a request or demand alone, even if exercisable at any time, does not establish that trigger. Survival requires express continuation after termination, expiration, or completion; a contract duration, remedy, severability rule, or enforceability provision is not survival. If survival is stated by section or subject, read and cite the referenced operative obligations with the survival clause. Post-agreement possession is supported whenever an express exception permits or requires retention after an otherwise applicable return-or-destruction duty, including an archival copy or retention because disposition is infeasible. It is opposed when the controlling unit exhaustively requires all information and copies to be returned or destroyed with no retention route. A bare return duty that does not settle later possession is NotMentioned. Cite the complete trigger-and-disposition unit and every qualification changing retention; omit certification or administrative text unless it narrows the substantive duty.

Inspect the receiving party's specific authority to make, reproduce, duplicate, or record a copy. Support requires affirmative operative permission, such as copying reasonably necessary for the stated purpose. A default prohibition on copying or reproduction opposes the hypothesis even when copying could occur with prior consent; a consent mechanism is not present permission unless another provision affirmatively authorizes the relevant copying. Do not infer creation authority from use, access, possession, recordkeeping, reducing information to writing, delivery or return of existing copies, or permission to retain one existing archival copy. When a prohibition contains an internal copying exception, cite both the prohibition and the exception if both define the permission; otherwise cite only the operative actor, copying verb, modality, and controlling condition. If the document addresses neighboring handling acts without settling creation of copies, return NotMentioned.

Read the governing exclusions or limitations and keep the two provenance routes separate. Independent-development support requires a clause saying the receiving party developed the information independently, normally without using, accessing, referring to, or relying on protected information. Prior possession, authorized use, a substantive information category, a warranty disclaimer, or receipt from another source does not establish development. Third-party-acquisition support requires receipt, disclosure, or lawful obtainment by the receiving party from a third party entitled to provide the information and not bound by the relevant restriction. A clause merely saying the disclosing party gave information to another person, or that information was independently developed, does not establish third-party acquisition. Cite the exclusion introduction when it supplies the consequence, the exact provenance prong, and any proof, no-use, lawful-source, or no-confidentiality condition. An express prohibition on the same route is Contradiction; absence of the exact route is NotMentioned.

Identify the disclosing actor, each expressly permitted recipient class, the information, purpose, need-to-know limitation, and confidentiality conditions. Because the employee hypothesis concerns some employees, a whitelist limited to necessary or authorized employees supports it; do not treat that limitation as opposition. For third parties, support requires at least one expressly permitted external or potentially external class, such as agents, representatives, consultants, advisers, affiliates, or another approved class. A whitelist containing such a class still supports the hypothesis when employees are listed alongside it and when need-to-know, written-undertaking, or recipient-liability conditions apply. A whitelist limited to employees, officers, or directors opposes the broader third-party-sharing statement, as does an operative outside-disclosure prohibition with no standing external-class exception. Merely allowing the recipient to request discretionary approval for a future outsider is not present permission. Read a general prohibition together with its exceptions before deciding. Cite the operative whitelist and every eligibility or responsibility condition that defines it; for opposition cite the restrictive unit establishing that outsiders are excluded, not unrelated security provisions.

Look for operative language that the agreement or disclosure grants the receiving party no license, title, interest, ownership, immunity, or other right in the confidential information or associated intellectual property. Express retained or exclusive ownership can support the no-right conclusion when it directly negates acquisition by the recipient; read scoped exceptions and any affirmative grant before deciding. An affirmative grant opposes the hypothesis only when it gives the receiving party a right in the same protected object. Do not infer a non-grant from a confidentiality definition, nondisclosure duty, permitted-use restriction, entire-agreement clause, remedy, disclaimer, or no-warranty language. Cite every independently operative ownership or non-grant sentence that contributes to the conclusion, but exclude warranty, accuracy, commercialization, or administrative language unless it itself grants or withholds the relevant right. If neither a grant nor a non-grant is expressed, return NotMentioned.

Match actor, conduct, object, polarity, trigger, duration, and exceptions exactly. Limited use is supported only by an operative sole-purpose, necessary-purpose, or no-other-purpose restriction; nondisclosure, confidentiality, ownership, or a definition alone does not restrict use. Cite all independently operative use restrictions and any incorporated purpose or exception needed to delimit them, but omit adjacent security and disclosure provisions. Compelled-disclosure notice requires notice or consultation responsive to a legal, regulatory, court, governmental, or comparable compulsory demand; breach, loss, incident, or unauthorized-disclosure reporting is not equivalent. Cite the compulsory-disclosure trigger and notice duty, plus a governing exception introduction only when it supplies their legal effect. Reverse engineering requires an express prohibition on reverse engineering, disassembly, decompilation, or an expressly equivalent act directed to the protected object; never infer it from identifiability, privacy, no-copy, ownership, no-license, or limited-use terms. No solicitation requires an express prohibition on soliciting, inducing, enticing, employing, or retaining the specified employees or representatives; contacting sources, using names, advertising, or disclosure restrictions do not qualify. Express permission for the same conduct is Contradiction; neighboring regulation or silence is NotMentioned. Include a qualification or duration only when it changes the responsive duty.

Read the complete definition and every alternative route by which information becomes protected; read an operative nondisclosure provision separately when testing confidentiality of the agreement or negotiations. For explicit identification, support requires every protected route to depend on marking, designation, description, oral or later written confirmation, or another identification condition stated in the document. Oppose if any blanket, nature-based, circumstances-based, or reasonable-person route protects information without that condition; an illustrative subject list is not itself an identification rule. For technical-only scope, support when the exhaustive definition is confined to substantively technical material such as formulas, software, engineering information, or technical data. Oppose when any included route expressly covers non-technical subjects such as business, financial, personnel, contractual, customer, or marketing information. Generic undefined references to confidential, proprietary, non-public, or business-related information do not alone settle exclusivity. Oral coverage requires express oral, verbal, visual, observed, spoken, or comparable non-tangible disclosure language, or an oral-confirmation mechanism; do not infer it from a subject category, discussions, meetings, or communications. Agreement-confidentiality requires an operative duty covering the agreement, its existence, its contents or terms, the fact or status of negotiations, or discussions about the transaction; an entire-agreement clause, governing-law term, remedy, or contemplated discussion is insufficient. Treat a prohibition as support for the confidentiality hypothesis, not opposition. For evidence, cite every definition route needed to resolve an all-routes or exclusivity claim; cite each independently included non-technical category that disproves technical exclusivity. For oral coverage, cite the form language and only grammar needed to establish its scope. For agreement-confidentiality, cite both the protected subject and the operative duty or prohibition. Exclude unrelated examples and administrative provisions.

operations.rationale: The parent lacked a positive rule for technical-only definitions and did not sufficiently separate definition-only hypotheses from agreement-confidentiality duties. The contrasts include an exhaustive formulas-only definition supporting nda-2, many definitions with enumerated non-technical routes opposing it, and repeated polarity errors where operative secrecy of negotiations or agreement terms was mislabeled as contradiction.

guidance.evidence_criterion: Analyze separately the triggering event, obligated actor, disposition command, retention exception, and survival language. Return-or-destroy upon termination is supported only when termination, expiration, completion or abandonment of the stated purpose, failure to proceed, cessation of services, or another express relationship-ending event itself activates the duty. A request or demand alone is insufficient. A clause conditioned on a request made at termination is also insufficient unless another branch independently mandates disposition when the relationship ends; by contrast, an end-event branch joined disjunctively with a separate request branch supports the hypothesis. Survival requires express continuation of identified obligations after termination, expiration, completion, or another stated endpoint. A fixed contract term, a period measured only from execution or disclosure, an equitable remedy, severability, or continued enforceability does not itself establish survival. When survival is stated by section or subject, read and cite the referenced operative obligations with the survival clause. Post-disposition possession is supported by an express exception allowing or requiring retention despite an applicable return-or-destruction command, including an archival or compliance copy, ordinary backup media, or continued possession because disposition is infeasible. It is opposed when the controlling command exhaustively requires all information and copies to be returned or destroyed and supplies no retention route, whether that command is triggered by an endpoint or a request. A bare return duty that is not exhaustive does not settle later possession. Cite the complete trigger-and-command sentence across all spans, together with every exception that changes retention or feasibility. Include certification, timing, or notice text only if it conditions the substantive disposition or retention result.

operations.rationale: Observed answers repeatedly treated request-only return clauses as termination duties and missed retention exceptions. The sources distinguish a duty automatically activated by an endpoint from one effective only if requested, while separately treating exhaustive all-copy commands as opposition to later possession and archival, backup, or infeasibility clauses as support.

guidance.evidence_criterion: Identify the disclosing actor, each expressly authorized recipient class, the protected information, purpose, need-to-know limit, and confidentiality or responsibility conditions. For employee sharing, support requires an operative permission covering at least some of the receiving party's employees; a whitelist restricted to necessary, designated, or authorized employees still supports the hypothesis. An express prohibition on disclosure to any person, with no employee exception, opposes it; mere silence about employees is NotMentioned. For third-party sharing, support requires a standing permission for at least one external or potentially external class such as agents, consultants, professional advisers, counsel, representatives, contractors, or subcontractors. Conditions such as need-to-know status, a written undertaking, recipient liability, or confidentiality training do not negate that permission. Affiliate status alone, or permission limited to an affiliate's employees, officers, or directors, does not establish the tested external professional or agent class. A whitelist confined to employees, officers, or directors opposes third-party sharing, as does a general outsider prohibition without a standing external-class exception. A mechanism allowing the receiving party to seek or obtain discretionary consent for a future outsider is not present permission. Read general prohibitions together with all exceptions before deciding. For support, cite the operative whitelist and each condition that defines who may receive the information; cite a governing introduction only when it supplies the permission's actor or legal effect. For opposition, cite all operative clauses that collectively restrict the whitelist or exclude outsiders, but omit unrelated security, ownership, and use provisions.

operations.rationale: The parent treated affiliates as a sufficient third-party class, conflicting with the observed opposition where disclosure reached only affiliate personnel, and it did not expressly state the employee-side opposition rule. Contrasts also show that agents, advisers, consultants, representatives, contractors, and subcontractors are qualifying external classes even when stringent conditions apply.
